newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Slovakia says it ready to join NATO.
newsitem.headline: Slovakia says it ready to join NATO.

text.p: Slovakia, appealing to be included in the first wave of new NATO members, on Thursday rebuffed criticism of its treatment of minorities, saying it was doing more for ethnic rights than some NATO states.
Slovak Foreign Minister Pavol Hamzik told a news conference that a proposed law protecting minority languages was all that was needed to improve human rights further in Slovakia.

The standards enjoyed by minorities "is higher than in some NATO countries, and certainly higher than in some (NATO) candidate countries neighbouring Slovakia, so we don't see the need to go further," he said.
"I don't say there are not a few points we have to improve ...but to have this possibility we have to have equal trust with our neighbours," he added.
The Bratislava government of Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar wants to be included in the first wave of ex-communist states to join the NATO military alliance, probably next year.
Slovakia's neighbours, Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, are viewed as frontrunners for membership. Slovenia has also been mooted for possible early entry.
"We are convinced we have done a lot of work and satisfied the criteria expected of the other candidates," Hamzik said.
In his address earlier to the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), Hamzik said it was crucial for the stability of central Europe for Slovakia to join NATO soon.
"The Slovak Republic still finds itself in...an inconvenient and historically risky security vacuum," Hamzik said in a speech to the OSCE's Vienna-based permanent council.
"We do not want to be a bridge to the East...The Slovak Republic has an eminent interest in joining NATO in the first wave along with our neighbours," he added.
Hamzik said Slovakia had embraced democracy, a market economy and adherence to human rights, but the process of change was still continuing and strengthening.
NATO and the European Union insist that former East Bloc countries must settle disputes with their neighbours before having any chance of being accepted into the two organisations.

The inclusion of Slovakia in the 16-member Atlantic alliance as early as next year appears to have stalled following growing concern over the treatment of its minorities, in particular the 600,000-strong ethnic Hungarian community.
Hamzik said Slovakia was concerned about separatism in the region, resulting from the breakup of former Yugoslavia.
"This...makes us cautious and this is the real danger to the security and stability in the region," he said.
The U.S. State Department said on October 3 that Washington was concerned about indications that the Slovak government's commitment to democracy had been weakening.
Hamzik told reporters in Vienna that the U.S. criticism of Bratislava's treatment of minorities had been mentioned during his visit to Washington earlier this month.
